newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Mining town hopes for revenge at British election.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Mining town hopes for revenge at British election.

text.p: The people of Barnsley have long and embittered memories, and many are viewing the prospect of a British election with glee.
If opinion polls are right, Britain's Conservative government will be thrown out after 18 years in power and, for this northern English town, it will be sweet revenge.
Barnsley has fared badly in the last two decades. Once the prosperous heart of Britain's coal industry, 14 percent of its working population is now jobless, twice the national average.
Most of those who do have jobs are poorly paid or work part time. Crime has soared and neighbours now rob one another in a town once known for its community spirit, police say.
The town centre has been spruced up in recent years with a new shopping mall, but the plethora of discount shops and the paucity of shoppers betrays Barnsley's widespread poverty.
The town's outskirts are a mass of shabby housing estates and there are few in Barnsley who don't blame the Conservatives for their town's decline.
"Labour must win this time. Its not just Barnsley, the whole country is in a terrible state," said a middle-aged woman out shopping in the sparsely-populated city centre.
A young mother agreed. "Labour would mean better education and more equal opportunities for him," she said, nodding towards her baby son in his pram.
Theirs are widely-held views in Barnsley. With its huge working class population, the town is traditional Labour territory.

At the last election in 1992, the Labour candidate won a majority of nearly 25,000 and at a by-election in December, the Conservative candidate came third, behind the minority Liberal Democrats, with just 1,300 votes.
MINERS STRIKE

Barnsley was built around the textile industry and when that went into decline, coal mining took over. But all 20 coalmines in the area were shut down in the 1980s and 90s after the miners lost a bitter, year-long fight against the closures.
It seemed almost a personal battle between the prime minister of the time, "Iron Lady" Margaret Thatcher, and Arthur Scargill, leader of the miners' union.
The 1984 strike began in Barnsley and spread into frequent pitched battles with police on the surrounding coalfields.
The miners were left battered, jobless and destitute after struggling for months with only donations from their union to live on.
For Thatcher it was a triumph which allowed her to extend her plans for sweeping privatisation to the coalmines and struck a death knell for trade union power.
Though Thatcher was deposed as party leader in 1990, there is little forgiveness for the Conservatives under the less abrasive John Major.
"The Tories (Conservatives) have got to go. They're too complacent, they're out of touch with the common people," said the wife of a former miner.

The Coalmine Communities Campaign (CCC), which represents the diminished coal industry and the former mining towns, is convinced the Conservatives haven't yet finished what it sees as the destruction of the coal industry.
CCC Director Professor Stephen Fothergill accuses Major's government of undercutting coal by giving the rival gas and nuclear industries unfair advantages.
If the Conservatives are returned to power in the election, which must be held by May 22, he believes that half of Britain's remaining 29 mines will be forced to close.
CAMPAIGN TO SAVE MINES
But the CCC is convinced Labour will win and that, despite the party's shift to the political centre in the past few years, it will step in to save the mines.
"We don't expect Labour to stand up and say Eureka' when they see our proposals," Fothergill told a roomful of miners in Pontefract, near Barnsley.
"They're not in the habit of saying anything to any group," he said to knowing laughter from people now familiar with Labour's wariness of backing any possible vote loser.
Labour's new pro-business image and its leader Tony Blair have caused deep suspicion in Barnsley. There are many who see Blair as a city-slicker with little notion of their troubles.
But Yorkshire people are pragmatic and old habits die hard.
New left wing parties have failed to seriously dent Labour's position because voters realise they have little chance of gaining power.
"It doesn't really matter who wins does it? they're all the same now," said a former miner. "I suppose I'll vote Labour though."
